comments.text:
Unlike GoT, armour was actually doing its job here... There was not a single sword cutting through armour, and the thrusts through mail were not that deep, which makes the prognosis far better than if the wound was deeper and wider (as both knives and swords tend to taper).
Also, the thrust to the throat isn't meant to target the throat per se, just like the thrust to the armpit. The prior is meant to go through the neck, causing an internal decapitation, and the latter is meant to hit the heart... I don't know enough to confirm it, but I suspect that it's easier to thrust from the front rather than the back to the neck, as in the latter case, the blade is more likely to skid off. All the tissue in front doesn't offer much protection, but it likely keeps the blade on track...

Late medieval helmets were very effective vs mace strikes it seems.

comments.text: Fun fact regarding boxing gloves: Modern injuries in boxing are actually way worse than in the old bare-knuckle days, purely because of boxing gloves. The reason being, gloves do less to protect the opponent, and more to protect the hand of the person wearing them. This protection allows a boxer to throw MUCH harder punches than if he were bare-knuckle, as they can do so with less/no danger of fracturing their hand with bone-on-bone contact, and those harder punches still deliver way more force even through the padding of the glove than the force one would receive from a much lighter punch from a bare-knuckle punch that's held back due to concern for breaking your own hand.

comments.text: I’m not sure if they would’ve had a substance like sunscreen back then, but as someone who loves historical clothing, Europeans (who inspire most of Westerosi culture) were generally covered up a lot more, almost always wearing jackets, long sleeves, long dresses and pants, gloves, and head coverings when outside across history. You might think this might get hot, and in some climates yes, but there’s also the factor that people in history weren’t using polyester fibers like we generally do. The natural fibers in the fabrics they would’ve worn would breathe much better and probably wouldn’t stink as much with added body odor. There’s also global warming destroying the protective ozone layer today that wasn’t happening nearly as much back then to consider. On top of all this, there’s also the factor of upper class people having a lot less manual labor to do and therefore being able to sit around in the shade or carry a parasol when outside, while members of the lower and working class didn’t have those luxuries, meaning they very well could’ve been sunburnt and it’s just not something typically mentioned in records because most records were written by or about the upper class
